explanation: The procedure does not set SET NOCOUNT ON at the top of its body, leaving row-count chatter enabled.
Transactions are used but SET XACT_ABORT ON is not set, allowing partial transaction application.
SELECT * couples callers to every current and future column of Sales.Orders.
SELECT TOP (10) without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary set of rows.
DISTINCT is unnecessary because OrderID is a primary key and already unique.
WITH (NOLOCK) can return uncommitted, missing, or duplicated rows.
YEAR on the indexed OrderDate column prevents a simple range seek.
Comparing int CustomerID with nvarchar variable forces implicit conversion and can cause index scans.
OR-based optional filtering makes cardinality estimation and seeking difficult.
LIKE pattern starting with % prevents a normal index seek on Comments.
NOT IN has surprising results when the subquery can produce NULL, returning no rows.
ISNULL on CustomerID makes the predicate non-sargable and prevents index seeks.
Arithmetic on OrderID prevents direct index matching.
Inequality predicate often scans broad portions of the table.
CROSS JOIN omits a join predicate and multiplies Orders by Customers.
Comma-separated tables with join conditions in WHERE obscure predicates and risk accidental cartesian joins.
Correlated scalar subquery executes a lookup for every qualifying order row.
Correlated EXISTS check runs per outer row instead of expressing a set join.
The same CASE expression is repeated in the select list and ORDER BY clause.
ORDER BY 2 refers to a select-list column position, which becomes fragile when the select list changes.
OFFSET/FETCH pagination has no stable ORDER BY tie-breaker and can return different rows across executions.
UNION performs needless duplicate removal between disjoint literal branches; use UNION ALL.
COUNT(*) > 0 is used when only existence is needed; use EXISTS instead.
SELECT @var = column silently accepts multiple rows and keeps the last value.
Use of a table variable may receive poor cardinality estimates on older compatibility levels.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates the temp-table schema implicitly instead of declaring it explicitly.
Cursor is used for work that can be expressed set-wise, causing row-by-row processing.
WHILE loop processes rows one at a time instead of using a set-based operation.
User input @CustomerID is concatenated directly into the dynamic SQL string before execution.
EXEC (@Sql) executes a dynamic string without parameterized inputs, risking injection and recompilation.
User input @OrderID is concatenated directly into the dynamic SQL string before execution.
EXEC sys.sp_executesql @Sql executes a dynamic string without parameterized inputs.
Explicitly created temporary table #Scratch is not dropped before the procedure ends.
CATCH block neither rethrows with THROW nor returns a failure status; the error is silently swallowed.
RAISERROR should be replaced by THROW for new error paths.
PRINT is buffered and unsuitable for structured diagnostics; use RAISERROR or return codes instead.
Business identifier 1 is embedded directly in SQL instead of being passed as a parameter.
Unlabelled date constant '20160101' is embedded in query logic; use a parameter or explicit conversion.
Date string converted without an explicit style parameter, relying on session settings.
COALESCE in the join predicate inhibits normal join optimization and index seeks.
Self-join retrieves information already available in the same row.
Sorting by the unselective text column Comments can cause a wide sort and memory grant issues.
Aggregates the entire fact-like OrderLines table without a restrictive filter.
Row-level predicate o.OrderID > 0 is placed in HAVING instead of WHERE.
ORDER BY on an aggregate result guaranteed to return one row is unnecessary.
MERGE has documented concurrency and correctness edge cases; use IF EXISTS/UPDATE/INSERT instead.
SET Comments = Comments evaluates to the current value, causing unnecessary logging and locking.
DELETE uses a broad non-key predicate on Quantity instead of a stable key.
WAITFOR DELAY intentionally blocks a worker; use asynchronous scheduling instead.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is not wrapped in a BEGIN TRY ... BEGIN CATCH block.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT ON changes session state and introduces fragile identity-management coupling.
System routine sp_who is invoked without schema qualification, risking name resolution issues.
SET ROWCOUNT changes session state and is not restored to its previous value.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (...) without an explicit column list risks schema change failures.
LIKE pattern with a leading % prevents a normal index seek on CustomerName.
User input @CustomerName is concatenated directly into the dynamic SQL string before execution.
EXEC sp_executesql @sql executes a dynamic string without parameterized inputs.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers lacks a WHERE clause and will update all rows.
Predicate on outer-joined table o.OrderDate in the WHERE clause effectively converts it to an inner join.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL is never true; use IS NULL instead of equals.
Scalar function dbo.GetCustomerType in the SELECT list forces row-by-row evaluation.
CATCH block inside a transaction does not roll back before handling the error.
Explicit table/index hint WITH (INDEX = 1) restricts plan selection and can cause performance issues.
Excessively nested subqueries (3+ levels) should be refactored to CTEs or temp tables.
SELECT * couples callers to every column of the function result and fails on schema changes.
